newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss government embraces NATO Partnership scheme.
newsitem.headline: Swiss government embraces NATO Partnership scheme.

text.p: The Swiss government said on Thursday it had agreed in principle to join NATO's Partnership for Peace programme and dismissed complaints that the step violated the country's tradition of strict neutrality.
"It should be clear to the rest the world that Switzerland will join the Partnership for Peace," government spokesman Achille Casanova said. "The political decision has been taken."

He said the government had instructed the foreign and defense ministries to draw up an application for joining the scheme, which aims to foster ties between the western military alliance and its former Warsaw Pact foes in eastern Europe.
Once parliament's foreign affairs committee has been informed, the decision -- agreed on Wednesday evening but announced only on Thursday -- can be made formal, he added.

Twenty-seven countries have already signed up for the programme, including neutrals Finland, Austria and Sweden. Their participation has triggered domestic debates that seem likely to be echoed in Switzerland.

Conservative parties here suggest that signing up is the first step toward joining the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, which has emerged from the Cold War as the bedrock of European security.
Others suggest voters should approve the step in a referendum, which could be forced if opponents gather 100,000 signatures under the Swiss system of direct democracy.
The right-wing Swiss Democrats (SD) party immediately challenged the government's decision.

"The Swiss Democrats especially criticise the fact that the Federal Council (government) once again wants to implement unilaterally such a wide-ranging military and political decision without a referendum," it said in a statement.
Casanova told Reuters the government was within its rights to make the decision and added he doubted it would be put to the voters. He dismissed suggestions Swiss neutrality was in danger.

"This step is absolutely compatible with Swiss neutrality," he said. "There are some areas (in the scheme) where we can take part, and there are areas where we cannot...Joining NATO would not be compatible with neutrality, but we are not doing that."
The Federal Council decided in January not to contribute to the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia because its official neutrality prevented it sending armed soldiers abroad.
But as current president of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), it is playing a direct role in organising Bosnia's first post-war elections and in promoting human rights.
